rows.text: Honestly this looks straightforward to get into — email/password, a disabled button until fields are filled, Enter-to-submit, live password rules. Nothing here would slow my team down, and the CRO-versus-in-house toggle at signup maps to exactly how I think about client segregation. The one thing that would trip people up is that MFA and SSO are half-here, half-promised, so I'd have to explain to my staff what is actually real today.

Honestly this reads as manageable — it's just an email-and-password card, and the disabled-until-filled button plus Enter-to-submit are the small conveniences my team expects. The MFA and workspace-creation branches are described plainly enough that I wouldn't dread rolling this out to my nine people. The one friction I foresee is the CRO-vs-own-company toggle at signup: my staff will need to be told to always pick "On behalf of clients," because getting that wrong at first-run has isolation consequences.

Honestly, the linear 10-step left rail with lock reasons is close to how I'd want a junior on my team walked through their first sequence, so the mechanics look manageable. What gives me pause is the sheer density on the transmission and lifecycle steps — receipt tiles, deficiency windows, sequence operators all on one screen — that's a lot to absorb without a person beside you. Medium effort for me; probably steeper for a less experienced associate.

The step-by-step rail with locked steps and lock reasons is the kind of hand-holding my junior associates would appreciate, and I like that the prerequisites are surfaced before Step 1 rather than discovered halfway through. That said, I evaluate for a team of nine who live in Vault and docuBridge, and a linear 10-step "journey" doesn't map to how we actually work parallel modules across several products at once. I'd want to know how much I can jump around versus being forced down the rail.

Honestly this reads as fairly approachable, more so than I expected. The New dossier flow is a straight two-field card, the placeholder-ID shortcut is sensible for early-stage products, and the type-the-ID-to-confirm gate on deletion mirrors what my team already expects from a controlled system. My only friction is that for someone managing nine people's work I'd want bulk views, filters and columns, not just a grid of tiles.

This looks straightforward enough that I wouldn't need to train my team on it — create a dossier, name the product, open it. The placeholder-ID option is smart, because in reality we're often building the shell weeks before Health Canada issues the actual Dossier ID through the REP request. The type-the-exact-ID-to-archive step is a bit of friction, but honestly that's the kind of friction I want on a destructive action.

The three-column layout with a section tree, teach boxes, and glossary tooltips reads like something my junior associates could pick up quickly, which matters when I'm onboarding nine people. What worries me is the Dossier ID format gate and the XML PM paste-and-validate step; those are the moments where a medium-comfort user fumbles, and I'd want to see the real error handling before I believe it's actually easy.

Once I got past the Dossier-ID format gate, the three-column layout with a section tree, a teach box, and clear Upload / Author / Mark N/A tabs is the kind of structure my team already thinks in, so navigation wouldn't be a hurdle. The form-filling itself looks straightforward, though the sheer density of glyphs, badges, chips and rail cards is a lot to absorb, and I'd want a half-day of hands-on before I'd let a junior loose on it. The ghost pre-fill that you must replace is a sensible pattern, but it adds a step people will forget under deadline pressure.

Conceptually this is familiar territory — a section tree with req/opt badges and gate flags maps cleanly onto how I already think about an eCTD lifecycle, so my team wouldn't be lost. The AI chat itself is about as easy as it gets: type context, review the reply, click to save. My only friction is the number of discrete steps to actually close a section — draft, use draft, then a separate attest click — which will feel like a lot of clicking across dozens of sections in a real dossier.

The layout is familiar enough — a section tree, a work panel, gate flags — it reads like a lighter version of the RIM tools my team already lives in, so I don't think the mechanics would trip anyone up. The chat-to-draft flow is genuinely simple: type context, review the streamed reply, click to save. My only friction is that the real work — reviewing an AI draft line-by-line against Health Canada guidance — still lands entirely on me, and the tool can't make that faster.

Honestly, this looks reasonably approachable — the side rail with Readiness, completeness check, and Sequences cards mirrors how I already think about a submission. The "How is X% measured?" and "What this does / does NOT check" toggles mean I'm not fighting a black box, which is where most of these tools lose me. My hesitation is the density: five module tabs, sequence operators, lifecycle chips, override flows — my junior associates would need a real training session, not just a tour.

The layout follows the same logic as the RIM tools my team already lives in — a dossier list, a sequence view, a readiness rail — so I could find my way around without much hand-holding. What I appreciate is that the percentage isn't just a number; the "How is X% measured?" expander tells me exactly which filing steps it counts, which is the first question my reviewers always ask. My only friction is the density of the right rail: readiness, completeness, sequences, technical check all stacked, so on a real dossier I'd want to know it scales without becoming a scroll marathon.

The page density is about right for someone who lives in RIM dashboards all day — portfolio cards, gate chips, fee status, module towers all in one view is the kind of at-a-glance triage I want. My hesitation is the sheer number of chip types crammed into each row; my more junior team members would need a legend, and I'd want to click through Registry and Correspondence a few times before it felt natural. Medium effort to onboard, but nothing here looks intimidating.

The layout follows the mental model I already carry — portfolio, registry, correspondence — so I could orient my team without much retraining, and the rollup strip for 30-day deadlines is exactly how I triage in my Excel trackers today. My worry is density: a single dossier row is carrying module tower, gate chip, fee chip, litigation clock, collaboration chips and two links, and with 80 active dossiers on screen that becomes a wall of chips my analysts will have to squint at. The correspondence page with three panels and the Form V / NOA register feels like the steepest part, but it maps cleanly to work we actually do.

If the walkthrough reads as truthfully as it's written, the guided step-rail with a resumable session and plain-language tooltips would be a relief for my junior staff, who currently drown in docuBridge's raw eCTD tree. The dossier-ID format enforcement and placeholder path match exactly how REP/CESG works, so onboarding wouldn't stall. That said, I've been burned by "guided" tools that get rigid when a real filing goes off the happy path, and I can't judge that from prose.

On paper this looks approachable — the guided step rail, resumable sessions, and plain-language tooltips over precise regulatory terms would lower the barrier for my junior associates, which is where I feel the most pain. My caution is that ANDS filings are genuinely complex, and a "guided end to end" wrapper can either flatten that helpfully or hide decisions I need to control, and I can't tell which until my team touches it.

Honestly this looks straightforward to get into — email, password, optional TOTP, and the disabled-until-filled button is standard stuff I use every day. The CRO-vs-own-company toggle at signup is a smart first-run question because I do file on behalf of clients and workspace isolation matters to me. Nothing here would slow me down.

This looks straightforward to get into — two fields, a disabled-until-filled button, Enter-to-submit, the MFA field only showing when relevant. That's all standard and I wouldn't stumble on it. The CRO-vs-own-company fork at signup is a nice touch that mirrors how I actually think about isolating client dossiers.

As someone who does document assembly and validation daily, this reads like it would be straightforward to move through — a 10-step left rail with lock reasons, a per-step gate, and validation on blur is the kind of guardrail I'd want, not fight. The placeholder-ID-continue path means I'm not dead in the water waiting on OSIP, which is realistic. My only ease concern is whether the guided linearity gets in my way when I need to jump around modules the way I do in eCTD Office, but nothing here looks hard.

If it works as written I'd move through it fast — the 10-step left rail with lock reasons and a "You're here" marker is exactly how I mentally track a sequence, and the placeholder-ID-then-continue pattern respects that I never have the Company ID and Dossier ID in hand on day one. My only worry is whether the gating is rigid; I sometimes need to jump around modules non-linearly, and a hard "Continue stays disabled until the gate clears" could fight my actual workflow.

This looks straightforward for someone like me who does assembly daily — the New dossier flow is only two fields and the placeholder-ID shortcut is genuinely thoughtful, since I often start prep before the real Dossier ID comes back from the REP request. Type-to-confirm on archive and a forced reason field are exactly the kind of friction I'd expect and want, not annoyances. Nothing here would slow me down.

This looks straightforward for someone like me. Creating a dossier is just an ID and a product name, and the placeholder path is a nice touch for when I'm still waiting on the Dossier ID Request to come back through REP. The confirm-by-typing-the-ID pattern for archiving is standard and I have no trouble with it.

The three-column layout with a section tree, req/opt badges and a glyph legend is exactly how I already think about eCTD, so I'd get oriented fast. The Dossier ID format enforcement (one letter + 6-7 digits) matches Health Canada's dossier numbering, which I appreciate, and the placeholder escape hatch is sensible. My only friction is the sheer density of affordances per section — upload, author, N/A, AI toggle, review-vs-HC, completeness checks — but that's the job, and I'd rather have them all in one place than in eCTD Office's scattered menus.

Honestly this looks manageable for someone like me who assembles sequences daily — three-column tree, glyph legend, req/opt badges, that's the mental model I already work in. The Dossier ID format hint (one letter + 6-7 digits) and the placeholder escape hatch are the kind of small thing that saves me a support ticket. My worry is the sheer number of affordances per section — upload/author/N/A tabs, ghost buttons, two different confirm mechanisms — it'll take a few dossiers before the muscle memory settles.

Honestly this looks fairly easy to navigate — the tree with req/opt badges and the three gate flags map cleanly to how I already think about eCTD completeness, and the chat flow is self-explanatory. The mode toggle between "Draft with AI" and "Fill the form" is a good touch because on some sections I'd never touch the AI. My only friction is that chat-based drafting is slower than pasting a template, so for high-volume sections I'd probably ignore it.

Mechanically this looks easy enough to operate — tabbed action bar, a chat box, a "Use this draft" button. As someone who does assembly daily, the flow of pick-section, choose Author in-app, chat, save, attest is intuitive and I wouldn't need hand-holding. My only friction is that AI drafting by conversation is slower and fussier than my usual practice of dropping in a controlled template, but the "Fill the form" fallback covers that.

The layout reads like something I'd get productive on fast — dossier tiles, M1-M5 tabs, a side rail with the cards I actually need for filing. The sequence/operator model with "working: 0001", lifecycle chips and make-active is exactly the mental model I use daily in eCTD Office, so I wouldn't have to relearn anything. Only friction is the density on that right rail, but that's fine for a power user.

Honestly this looks manageable for me — I live in sequences and lifecycle operators all day, so "0000/0001 working", new/replace/delete chips, and a purpose dropdown are my native vocabulary. The layout (section tree left, doc panel center, cards on a right rail) is close to how GlobalSubmit Review lays things out, so I wouldn't be lost. My only friction is the sheer number of cards stacked on that rail — readiness, completeness, sequences — I'd want to know I can collapse what I'm not using.

Honestly this reads like it'd be quick for me to navigate — cards, chips, rollup strips, provenance popovers, it's the kind of dense dashboard I live in daily. My worry isn't clicking around, it's that there's a lot of chip-soup crammed onto each row (module tower, gate chip, fee chip, litigation clock, collab chips) and I'd want to actually sit with it to see if it stays legible at 15 dossiers or turns into noise.

If this behaves like the walkthrough reads, it'd be easy enough for me — the portfolio, registry and correspondence split maps to how I already think, and the day-counters, module towers and gate chips are the kind of at-a-glance status I want. My worry is density: that's a lot of chips per row, and until I click around live I can't tell if it stays scannable across 40+ dossiers or turns into visual noise.

Honestly this reads like it'd be manageable for me — I do assembly and validation daily, so a three-column journey with a step rail, module tower, and a live readiness percentage maps cleanly onto how I already think about an eCTD backbone. The plain-language tooltips on acronyms don't help me personally, but they wouldn't get in my way. My only friction is that I can't judge how the guided rail behaves once a real sequence gets messy — lifecycle operators, replace/append, deficiency responses — and that's where guided tools usually fall apart.

Honestly this looks manageable — the three-column layout with a step rail, active card, and readiness view is how I'd want to work, and resuming a saved session matters when a sequence spans weeks. The Dossier ID format check (one letter + 6-7 digits) is exactly the kind of guardrail I fight with in eCTD Office. My only worry is whether the "guided journey" pushes me into a linear path when real ANDS prep is rarely sequential.

Honestly this looks pretty easy — it's just a normal sign-in card, and the fact that the button won't light up until I've filled both fields and I can just hit Enter to submit is what I'd expect. The signup step asking "Your own company" vs "On behalf of clients (CRO)" is nice because I actually am at a CRO, so I'd know to pick that one right away. Nothing here would make me stop and ask a senior.

Honestly this part looks straightforward. It's just a sign-in card, and the button staying greyed out until I fill both fields and Enter-to-submit is exactly how I'd expect it to work. The CRO vs. own-company toggle at signup would matter for me since we file for clients, and the password rules counting down live is a nice touch so I'm not guessing.

Honestly it looks manageable — the left rail with 10 steps and the "You're here" marker means I'd always know where I am, which is more than my Word templates give me. The padlock-with-a-reason thing is reassuring because right now when a senior tells me something's "not ready" I never know why. My worry is Step 1 alone crams in company ID, dossier ID, pathway questions, and a module builder link, so it might feel like a lot before I've even gotten going.

Honestly this looks manageable — the padlocks with lock reasons and the "You're here" marker mean I wouldn't have to guess what's next, which is exactly what I need since I usually ping a senior. The placeholder-ID path is a relief because right now I'd be stuck for two weeks waiting on the Company ID before I could even open the file. My only worry is 10 steps plus a 3D tower feels like a lot on screen at once, but I can toggle to the plain checklist, so fine.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable for me. The "New dossier +" button and the two-field card are simple, and the "No ID yet? Start with a placeholder" option is a relief because on my first filings I never have the real Dossier ID early on. Typing the exact ID plus a reason to archive feels like a few extra steps, but I'd rather that than delete something by accident.

Honestly this looks fairly easy to follow — it's basically a folder of my products with a big "New dossier +" button, which maps to how I think about my two filings. I like that I don't need a real Dossier ID to start; the placeholder option means I could set up my draft before the CESG paperwork clears, which is exactly the situation I'm in right now. The inline card with just two fields wouldn't intimidate me.

Honestly it looks manageable — the three-column layout with a section tree, the glyph legend right there, and the tabbed "Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A" choices map to how I actually think about a filing. The Dossier ID format rule with a worked example and the "no ID yet, use a placeholder" escape hatch is a relief, because on my first two ANDS I never had the ID sorted early. My only worry is the sheer number of chips and cards — module tabs, viewer, audit, portfolio, journey, plus three columns of controls — so there's a lot to scan before I know where to click.

Honestly, this feels like a lot to take in for someone still learning. The three-column layout with the section tree, glyphs, badges and right rail is probably workable once I get used to it, but the sheer number of chips, tabs and tags on one screen is intimidating on first read. That said, having the dossier known-facts pre-filled and a form to fill instead of wrestling a Word template is a big relief compared to how I work now.

Honestly this looks pretty approachable — I like that it's a chat where I just describe the submission and it asks me for what it needs instead of me staring at a blank template. The section tree with req/opt badges and the progress bar tells me where I am, which is more than my Word-on-a-shared-drive setup gives me. The one thing that would slow me down is knowing what to type first; the example placeholder helps, but I'd still want to know how much detail is "enough."

Honestly this looks pretty manageable — I like that there's a clear path: pick a section, hit "Author in-app," and just chat. The idea that it asks me for details instead of leaving blanks is great, because half my job right now is figuring out what a senior would expect me to put in a blank. My only worry is the section tree with all the glyphs and badges — req/opt, the AI star, gate flags — feels like a lot to decode on day one before I know what's normal.

Honestly it looks manageable once someone shows me around, but that's a lot of cards on one screen — Readiness, Draft completeness, Sequences all stacked in a side rail. As someone still learning, I'd worry about clicking Export on the wrong sequence, though the fact that it fails closed and won't let me export without passing validation is reassuring. The "How is X% measured?" and "What this does / does NOT check" toggles would help me a lot since I can't always tell what a percentage actually means.

Honestly it's a lot of cards and chips to take in on one screen, but the layout follows a logic I could learn — readiness, then the completeness check, then sequences, then export. The "Do this next →" button when something is blocked is exactly what I need as someone still figuring out the steps, so I wouldn't be stuck guessing. I'd probably lean on a senior the first time, but after one walkthrough I think I could do it.

Honestly this looks like a lot to take in on one screen — chips everywhere, day-counters, provenance popovers, three separate panels on the Correspondence page. But most of it maps to things I already do by hand, so the actual actions (register a product, ingest a notice, tick the annual checklist) seem straightforward once someone shows me where to click. The portfolio "at a glance" cards and the "soonest first" deadline strip are the kind of thing I'd actually use daily.

Honestly this looks manageable — it's organized like a dashboard with rows and chips, which isn't far off from scanning a shared drive folder, just tidier. The Portfolio page tells me at a glance what's ready and what's blocked, and I like that "soonest first" deadline strip because chasing due dates is half my job right now. My worry is the sheer number of chips and panels (gate, fee, litigation clock, collaboration, provenance popovers) — I'd need someone to walk me through what half of them mean before I'd move quickly.

Honestly this looks manageable for me. The "Start my submission" path with a step rail and everything explained in plain language is exactly what I need since I'm still learning the terminology, and the fact that it saves and resumes my session takes a lot of pressure off. The three-column layout with a 3D tower sounds a bit busy, but I'd just toggle to the plain checklist view.

Honestly this reads like it would be manageable for me, which is saying something because ANDS work usually terrifies me. The step rail plus a card in the middle sounds like it holds your hand, and the fact that it resumes my saved session and saves progress automatically matters a lot when I get pulled off things constantly. The 3D tower I'd probably ignore and just toggle to the plain checklist, but I'm glad that's an option and not forced on me.

Honestly, this reads like something I could manage without much hand-holding — a single card, two fields, a button that stays greyed out until I fill both in. The signup toggle asking "Who are you filing for?" is a sensible fork, and the live password-rule counter means I'm not guessing why it won't accept my password. My only friction is the MFA step; I'd want our IT person walking me through the authenticator app the first time, but the instructions are spelled out well enough.

The sign-in card itself looks simple enough that I could manage it without hand-holding, and I appreciate that Enter submits and the button waits until both fields are filled. What gives me pause is the sheer amount packed into the Account and security page, but at least I'm not being asked to do all of it at once just to log in.

Honestly this looks manageable for someone in my position — a locked left rail with ten steps and a "you're here" marker is the kind of linear checklist I already live by in my SOPs. What I appreciate is that gates stay disabled until they clear, so I can't accidentally skip a control. My worry is the up-front density: the prerequisites card, the placeholder-ID logic, and all the receipt tiles are a lot to absorb before I've done anything, and at my tech comfort level I'd want a colleague walking me through the first pass.

The prerequisites card up front is honestly the first thing in a cloud tool that's spoken my language — it tells me the Company ID and Dossier ID take real weeks and lets me proceed on a placeholder, which is how work actually happens. Ten steps with lock reasons and a "you're here" marker is manageable. My worry is the density: 3D towers, tiles, panels for lifecycle and sequences — that's a lot to absorb, and I'd want to see the plain "Checklist" printable table by default, not the 3D view.

I could find my way through it, but I'd be leaning on that checklist table, not the animated tower.

Honestly this reads like something I could navigate without much hand-holding, which surprises me for a cloud tool. Creating a dossier is two fields and a button, and the placeholder-ID option means I'm not blocked waiting on Health Canada to issue the real number. The typed-confirmation-plus-reason step to archive is more work, but that's exactly the kind of friction I want on a destructive action.

Honestly this reads like something I could navigate without much hand-holding, which is not what I expected from a cloud tool. The "New dossier +" flow is short, the placeholder-ID option means I'm not blocked waiting on Health Canada, and the glossary tooltips on eCTD, Module 1, REP and CESG at point of use would save my juniors a lot of "what does this mean" questions. The type-the-ID-to-confirm step on delete is exactly the kind of friction I want, not an annoyance.

Honestly, this looks like a lot to absorb — three columns, five module tabs, glyph legends, badges, tabs-within-tabs. I've spent 15 years in QA and I could learn it, but I'd want an SOP and a day of hand-holding before I trusted my own clicks. The upside is that the ID format and the "start with a placeholder" escape hatch are spelled out, which spares me guessing.

Honestly, this looks dense. The three-column layout with a section tree, glyphs, badges, and a right rail full of cards is a lot to take in, and I'd need someone to walk me through it the first time. That said, the workflow itself — pick a section, see what Health Canada wants, upload or author, run a check — follows a logical order I recognize from assembling submissions, so once I learned the pattern I think I could work it.

Honestly, the chat-to-draft idea reads as approachable for someone at my comfort level — I type plain facts about the sponsor and it asks me for the rest rather than leaving blanks, which I appreciate. The multi-step gauntlet (Author in-app, then a Draft-with-AI toggle, then Use this draft, then a separate attest button) is a lot of clicks and states to track, but each step is labelled, so I could follow it. The "Fill the form" fallback when there's no API key reassures me I'm not stuck.

Honestly, this looks more approachable than I expected — clicking a section, seeing "What Health Canada needs here," and choosing between uploading, authoring, or marking N/A is a workflow I recognize from my document vault. The chat box asking me questions instead of leaving blanks is fine, though I'd be slow with it because I'd stop and check every claim. The two-step "Use this draft" then "I have reviewed this" is extra clicking, but I actually appreciate that it forces a pause.

Honestly, this looks like a lot of cards and chips crammed onto one screen, and I'd need to sit with it a while before I trusted where things were. That said, the fact that "Export blocked" hands me a "Do this next" button and lists the exact failing leaf and rule id means I'm not left guessing, which is more than I can say for most tools. For someone like me who works off SOPs, I'd want a one-page checklist mapping these steps before I let my team near it.

Honestly, reading through this I get the sense it would take me a while to find my footing, but the structure is logical enough — tiles, module tabs, a readiness card, a completeness check. I'd want to sit with it and walk through one dossier before I trusted my hands on it. The number of cards and toggles on that right rail is a lot to absorb at once, but nothing here looks arbitrary.

Reading it, the layout sounds orderly enough — cards, rows, chips, a due-date rollup — and I could probably find a dossier and its status without much fuss. But there's a lot of terminology packed into each row, and I'd want to sit with it before trusting myself to read those chips correctly. For someone like me who works off paper SOPs, the density is a bit much at first glance.

I'd need training on it.

Reading this, the layout sounds like a lot of chips and strips packed onto one screen, but the actual actions are simple enough — open a dossier, ingest a notice, tick a checklist item. I'd want to see it hands-on before judging, because dense dashboards like this either click for me quickly or bury the one number I actually need. The pre-filled dossier field and the "no dossiers yet" fallback tell me someone thought about the empty states, which I appreciate.

Reading through it, the guided step-rail with everything saved automatically and plain-language tooltips on the acronyms sounds manageable, which matters because the people assembling these on my team aren't regulatory specialists. The 3D "submission tower" I'd toggle straight to the plain checklist view — I don't need eye candy, I need to see what's done. My real concern is the initial setup and self-hosting inside our own environment; that's not something I do myself, so "easy" depends heavily on IT standing it up correctly.

Reading it, this looks manageable — the step rail, the readiness percentage, and the plain-language tooltips on the acronyms would help someone on my team who assembles the package. I'm less sure about the 3D "submission tower" gimmick, but I'm relieved they let you toggle it to a plain checklist, because that's what I'd actually use. My bigger concern is always whether the guided flow lets people skip steps they shouldn't, and I can't tell that from a walkthrough.

Honestly, for what it is — a sign-in and account page — it's straightforward and I'd have no trouble. Two fields, a disabled button until both are filled, Enter-to-submit, the CRO-vs-own-company fork at signup is exactly the distinction I live with daily since I file for six or seven sponsors. The forgot-password demo-code reveal dance is a bit fiddly, but that's a demo artifact, not something I'd hit in production.

This is straightforward enough that I wouldn't think twice — email, password, optional 6-digit code, all standard. The signup fork asking "Your own company" vs "On behalf of clients (CRO)" is exactly the right question and it maps to how I actually work, one isolated workspace per client. The one friction point is that changing a password means signing out and going through the forgot-password flow, which feels clumsy, but it's not a dealbreaker.

The layout is straightforward enough — a left rail of ten steps, a step card, a readiness panel — and I'd find my way around without much trouble. What I appreciate is that it front-loads the two external prerequisites and lets me proceed with a placeholder rather than blocking me, which is how the real timing actually works. My only friction is the sheer density of the transmission and lifecycle panels; there's a lot on screen at once, and a less experienced preparer would be overwhelmed.

Honestly this looks manageable — the ten-step left rail and the "You're here" / padlock states tell me where I am, which is more than my Word checklists do. My worry is the orientation form gating: if Continue stays disabled until "the gate clears" and I can't see exactly which field is blocking me, I'll be hunting. But letting me start with a placeholder Dossier ID and continue is exactly how the real world works, so I wouldn't be stuck waiting.

Honestly this reads as manageable — the create flow is two fields and a button, which is about as simple as it should be. The placeholder-ID escape hatch is smart because half my clients come to me before they've filed their Dossier ID Request, so I can start building without a real ID. Type-to-confirm on archive plus a required reason is a bit of friction, but it's the right kind of friction for a destructive action.

This reads as straightforward for someone like me who lives in these dossiers daily — a New dossier button, two fields, and a clear placeholder path for when you don't yet have a real ID. The confirm-by-typing-the-ID pattern for archiving is a bit of friction, but it's the right kind, and Escape/backdrop close means I'm not trapped. Nothing here would slow me down.

Honestly this would take me some ramp-up, but not because it's badly built — there's a lot of scaffolding here: module tabs, a section tree with glyphs, req/opt badges, upload vs author vs N/A, ghost pre-fill, two different confirm mechanisms. The glyph legend and the "What Health Canada needs here" teach box would help me orient a junior, but for me the density is high on first pass. Once I learned the pattern I'd move quickly, since it maps onto how I already think in eCTD sections.

Honestly, this looks like a lot of screen to parse before I'd feel oriented — three columns, glyph legends, chips, badges, tabs within tabs. But the structure mirrors how I actually think: module tree on the left, section content in the center, readiness flags on the right, which is close to how I move through eCTD in eValidator and my own checklists. The Dossier ID format enforcement (one letter + 6-7 digits) is a nice touch since I've watched sponsors fumble that. I'd be slow the first hour, competent by the afternoon.

The workflow reads as reasonably straightforward — click a section, choose "Author in-app", chat, then "Use this draft". I've never drafted a dossier by chatbot, so the conversational bit is unfamiliar, but the gated steps are laid out in sequence and I'd manage. The one thing that would slow me down is not knowing what the AI actually asks for versus what I'm expected to volunteer.

Honestly this reads as fairly usable — the tabs (Upload / Author in-app / Mark N/A) map to how I actually triage a section, and defaulting AI mode to chat that asks for missing details rather than dumping blanks is sensible.
